title: Addressing Modes
summary: How an instruction says where an operand actually lives — the modes that show up in every ISA comparison question.

slides.markdown:
An **addressing mode** is the rule an instruction uses to compute where an operand actually lives. The same instruction shape (`load`, `add`) can point at wildly different places depending on which mode it uses: a constant baked into the instruction, a register, or a memory address built from a formula.

This matters because addressing modes are how ISAs express **pointers, arrays, and structs** at the hardware level — a compiler picks the mode, not the human writing C.

Every mode trades off **flexibility** against **decode/execution cost** — richer modes need more hardware work to compute the effective address.

slides.subTitle: Immediate and register
slides.markdown:
**Immediate addressing** — the operand *is* a constant embedded directly in the instruction: `addi $t0, $t0, 5` adds the literal `5`, no memory or extra register read needed.

**Register addressing** — the operand lives in a register named by the instruction: `add $t0, $t1, $t2` reads `$t1` and `$t2` directly.

Both are fast because there's **no memory access and no address computation** — the value is either already sitting in the instruction or already loaded into a register.

slides.subTitle: Direct and register-indirect
slides.markdown:
**Direct addressing** — the instruction contains the actual memory address to access: `load r1, [0x4000]`. Rare in practice since most addresses aren't known until run time.

**Register-indirect addressing** — a register holds a pointer, and the instruction dereferences it: `load r1, [r2]` reads from whatever address `r2` currently contains. This is exactly how a compiled C pointer dereference (`*p`) becomes a machine instruction.

Register-indirect is the workhorse for any code that walks linked structures — lists, trees, arbitrary pointers.

slides.subTitle: Indexed and base+offset
slides.markdown:
**Base + offset (displacement) addressing** — effective address = a base register + a constant offset: `load r1, 8(r2)` reads the memory 8 bytes past whatever `r2` points to. This is exactly how a struct field access (`p->field`) compiles.

**Indexed addressing** — effective address = base + an index register (often scaled by element size): perfect for array indexing (`a[i]`), where the index changes at run time but the base array pointer doesn't.

Both let one instruction encode a whole family of addresses instead of needing a separate instruction per offset.

slides.subTitle: PC-relative addressing
slides.markdown:
**PC-relative addressing** computes the effective address as an offset from the **current program counter**, not an absolute address: `beq r1, r2, +12` branches to "12 bytes past this instruction," wherever that ends up being in memory.

This is what makes **position-independent code** possible — a shared library can be loaded at a different address every run (a security measure, ASLR) and its internal branches and data references still work unchanged, because they're all relative to *themselves*, not to fixed addresses.

Almost every branch instruction in every ISA uses PC-relative addressing for exactly this reason.

Base + index + displacement is the most general common form — the hardware runs a small formula before it even touches memory:

![Effective address computed from base register plus scaled index register plus displacement](assets/effective-address.svg)

This single addressing mode covers array-of-structs access (`arr[i].field`) in one instruction: `base` is the array's start, `index` is `i` (scaled by struct size), and `displacement` is the field's offset within the struct.

slides.markdown:
Addressing-mode richness is one of the clearest fingerprints of ISA philosophy:

| | RISC (e.g. MIPS, RISC-V) | CISC (e.g. x86) |
|---|---|---|
| Modes supported | A handful — register, immediate, base+offset | Dozens — every combination of base/index/scale/displacement |
| Decode cost | Low — one predictable formula | Higher — more cases to compute |
| Compiler work | Must synthesize complex access from simple modes | Can often express access in one instruction |

Decide by asking: does simple, uniform decode (RISC) matter more than expressing complex access patterns compactly (CISC)? RISC ISAs bet the compiler can compensate cheaply; that bet mostly paid off.

How `a[i]` in C actually compiles, assuming `a`'s base address is in `$s0`, `i` is in `$s1`, and elements are 4 bytes:

```c
int x = a[i];
```

```asm
sll  $t0, $s1, 2      # t0 = i * 4  (scale index by element size)
add  $t1, $s0, $t0    # t1 = base + scaled index
lw   $t2, 0($t1)      # load from effective address -> x
```

On an ISA with true indexed+scaled addressing, this collapses closer to one instruction — but the *effective address computation* is identical either way.

slides.subTitle: Folding the pointer bump into the access
slides.markdown:
**Auto-increment/decrement addressing** updates the pointer register as a side effect of the access itself: `load r1, [r2]+` reads from `r2`'s address and then bumps `r2` to point past it, in one instruction. Some ISAs also support pre-decrement (`[--r2]`) for the opposite direction.

This is exactly the primitive behind stack push/pop (decrement-then-store, load-then-increment) and tight array/string traversal loops — instead of a separate `add` instruction to advance the pointer after every access, the addressing mode does it for free as part of the load or store. RISC-V and MIPS deliberately omit this mode to keep every instruction's effect predictable from decode alone; x86 and ARM's stack push/pop instructions bake it in directly.
